The $885/t price rally represented the sharpest rise in prices since February last year when prices traded up from $7190/t to $8430/t. Official prices (3m) averaged $5218/t in July, their highest level since September last year. During the early part of July and in the absence of any fresh fundamental news 3-month quotes traded lower on the back of a rising US dollar and increased pessimism regarding the pace of global economic recovery. Consequently, 3-month prices traded downwards from $5102/t at the end of June to $4823/t on the 9th July. However, from the 10th onwards market sentiment was buoyed by positive results from the Chinese and European auto sectors, better than expected Q2 corporate earnings from several of the major US banks and a generally more positive macro economic picture. _Price rise supported by positive results from the auto and banking sectors as well as supply side issues_ In China the Association of Automobile Manufacturers reported that car sales rose by 48% year on year in June and 5.3% month on month. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, Chinese vehicle production increased by 15% in H1 compared with the corresponding period in 2008. Meanwhile in Europe, Eurozone car registrations increased by 3% in June from a month earlier. This was significant because it represented the first such rise in 14 months. In the US, Goldman Sachs was the first major bank to report better-than-expected Q2 results which helped boost official (3m) quotes by $191/t on the 15th . J.P Morgan, Citibank and Bank of America followed suit in the following week which provided further support to prices. On the economic front, sentiment was buoyed by the release of data which indicated that economic growth in China had continued to gain momentum. Chinese GDP grew by a faster-than-expected 7.9% in Q1 from a year earlier. This compared with 6.1% year-on-year growth in Q1. Meanwhile industrial production jumped by 10.7% year on year in June. This followed annual growth of 8.9% in May and 7.3% in April. In addition, a whole spate of further mine disruptions came to light as evidenced by specific announcements (e.g. Collahuasi and Vale Inco) and Q2 company results (e.g. Inmet Mining and Quadra Mining – see Production) COPPER LME OPEN INTEREST vs COPPER PRICE

Between the 23rd and the end of the month (3m) quotes firmed further, reflecting better than expected US macro economic data, reaching the month’s high of $5708/t on the 31st . The general sentiment of the funds towards copper in the past month seems to have fallen broadly into two camps, i.e. those who have bought into the sustainable Chinese demand story and those who believe that Chinese demand has peaked and will be satisfied largely by existing inventory in the medium term. _Funds are cautiously optimistic towards copper_ Open interest on the LME trended higher in July, but fluctuated significantly, rising as prices increased, suggesting new long positions, and subsequently having fallen back on any sign of price weakness, indicating long liquidation. The data suggests that while sentiment has improved and further funds have flowed into copper, market participants remain nervous and will look to exit long positions as and when any negative triggers occur. The rise in copper prices through July has resulted in a shift in the shape of the forward curve, with near term prices rising more than those further out. At the start of the month the copper curve was in slight contango for the next twelve months and flat thereafter. The greater rise in near-term prices has pushed the forward curve into backwardation, indicating market expectations of some short-term tightness in the copper market. However, that prices have risen across the curve is likely a reflection of the improved market sentiment. As of the 30th , total exchange stocks increased by a net 6kt in July to 382.1kt. This represented the first monthly increase since February. In contrast to previous months, LME inventories increased by a net 15.2kt, to 280.9kt, while Comex and SHFE stocks fell by a net 4.2kt and 5kt to 50.1kt and 51.1kt respectively. The gain in LME inventories mainly reflected increases in warehouses in the USA (+13.4kt) and South Korea (+9.5kt). The latter increase is thought to be from material that was originally destined for China, being diverted to Busan. Inventories there rose by a net 9.4kt to 10.4kt and suggested that China’s demand for imported material was waning. According to anecdotal evidence the European physical copper market has been experiencing one of its quietest summer periods on record. That said one of the few bright spots has been Turkey where wire rod producers have been benefitting from stable orders for wire and cable from Iraq as the country’s infrastructure continues to be rebuilt. Thus grade A material in Turkey was fetching around $100/t. Elsewhere, Chilean and grade A cathode continued to trade between $70-90/t while Italian warrants commanded a slightly higher price of $90-100/t. This reflected tighter availability of material in the region. Finally, the price for standard grade material remained between $20-30/t. In the US, premia weakened slightly during July, slipping to 4-5c/lb delivered Midwest from 4.5-5.5c/lb previously. The lower level reflected a dearth of spot business and an increase in the availability of scrap. Similar to Europe, many traders and merchants believed that the slowdown in spot business ahead of the summer shutdown period was more pronounced than in previous years. Chinese premia also weakened during the month, falling from $130/t at the end of June to $80-$100/t at the time of writing. Improved scrap supplies were in part responsible for pushing premia levels lower. Last month we noted that 6000 containers of scrap material were held up in southern Chinese ports because of heightened inspection activities by the authorities. Latest reports suggest that at least half of these containers have now been cleared. Record refined copper imports in June were also responsible for suppressing premia. According to latest customs data, Chinese refined copper imports surged by 494% (+311kt) in June to yet another monthly all-time high. For H1 as a whole, refined imports totalled ~1.8Mt, up 184% (+1.1Mt) from a year ago. These high levels of imports were prompted by a favourable SHFE arbitrage over LME quotes for the majority of the six-month period. Chinese domestic prices were boosted by strong power cable production and by substantially reduced scrap availability. SHFE prices traded at an average of $197/t above LME quotes during H1. **ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS** The month of July has seen a continued improvement in a number of key economic indicators, although in most cases rising trends are starting from a very low base and simply indicate a lessening in the rate of contraction rather than a rebound in activity. The major exception is China, where indicators are pointing to acceleration in the rate of economic growth. Although positive in the short-run, the sustainability of this recovery remains uncertain given the poor economic performance of the developed world to date. The provisional estimate for Q209 GDP in China indicates a pick up in economic growth. GDP growth rose from a moderate 6.1% year on year in Q1 to 7.9% in Q2. This has been driven by a surge in government led investment, as exports continue to fall with demand in the rest of the world remaining lacklustre. Specifically, fixed asset investment in China surged 35% (year-on-year) in the first half of 2009, an impressive gain given the fall in foreign direct investment (which dropped 17.9% over the same period). However, the increase in investment (and its contribution to GDP growth) may have been somewhat overstated since the data include the value of land sales. _Economic indicators continue to improve…_ _…especially in China, but concerns remain_ ##### **FIXED ASSET INVESTMENT GROWTH IN CHINA** 35%

A significant contributor to the surge in investment, and hence economic activity, is the government’s $586bn stimulus package. This package has driven a boom in state-directed infrastructure projects, many of which had been put on hold over the past couple of years to help slow growth when overheating was considered the key risk. There has also been a significant increase in bank lending recently, which reached US$1.1 trillion in the first half of the year (equal to one-quarter of China’s total economic output). A relaxation of lending guidelines since November 2008 has helped drive bank lending, resulting in a 29% increase in M2 money supply in the year to June. The increase in liquidity does appear to have been feeding through to the Chinese consumer, with housing sales soaring and auto sales increasing by 48% in June from a year earlier. The authorities are indicating that they are looking to keep monetary policy fairly loose, but concerns have been raised that the flood of liquidity will fuel bubbles in house and equity prices, and lead to an increase in bad loans. The major risk for China is that the recovery will lose pace into the medium-term without an improvement in the economies of its major trading partners. Chinese exports in June were down by 21.4% from a year earlier. Government spending can only shield China’s economy from the global downturn

Although down by 17.9% year-on-year, German industrial production rose by 3.7% in May (month on month). This supported the rise in Germany’s Ifo business climate index which reached a nine month high of 87.3 in July. The Ifo’s ‘current conditions’ sub-index was also an improvement on June’s record low suggesting businesses now believe the worst of the recession may have passed. However, the Ifo’s ‘expectations’ sub-index remains subdued: businesses expect the economy to stabilise at a low level and for economic recovery to be slow and drawn out. Japanese industrial production continued to increase in May, albeit from a low base. Industrial production was 27.6% lower year on year in May but on a monthly basis it appears to have bottomed out. May’s industrial production was up 5.7% month on month and 14% from the February low. Recent growth in industrial output can be attributed to the very severe cut in output by producers that occurred in late 2008 and early 2009. The recent rebound is therefore more of an adjustment effect rather than a real, strong recovery. There have been signs of stabilisation in overseas demand, with shipments of environmentally friendly cars particularly strong, but stabilisation is at a low base and overall in June exports were down 37.5% year-on-year. May’s machinery orders were also down 38% on the year, and weak profit margins and excess capacity look set to keep capital investment subdued in the coming quarters. _Rate of contraction in US industrial output slows_ Turning to the US, industrial output declined by a further 0.4% in June, the slowest monthly decline since last autumn. For the second quarter as a whole, industrial production fell at an annualised rate of 9.9%, compared with 18.4% and 21.8% in 4Q08 and 1Q09 respectively. ### **CONSUMPTION** 

We have raised our global demand estimates quite significantly from our last monthly report.  The sharp rises, ~500kt for this year and next and ~400kt in 2011, solely reflect the increases we have made to our Chinese demand figures. Chinese consumption so far this year has been much stronger than many, ourselves included, expected.  The strong growth reflects both an increase in underlying demand, supported by the government’s stimulus packages, as well a shortage of scrap material.  According to latest trade data imports of copper scrap declined by ~40% in H1 from a year earlier.  This equated to a decline of ~250kt on a copper content basis, according to our calculations.  We now forecast a 20% increase in Chinese copper consumption this year, up from 5Mt in 2008 to ~6Mt.  However, this growth is not strong enough to offset contraction in demand outside of China.  Thus we forecast that global copper demand will decline by 0.8% this year to 17.8Mt.  In 2010 and 2011 global demand is expected to recover, increasing by 2.4% and 5.6% to ~18.2Mt and 19.2Mt respectively. 

A major support to underlying Chinese demand so far this year has been the ongoing investment within the power sector.  According to reports orders for power cable were very strong during the first four months of the year but weakened in May and June.  However, they are expected to pick up again in this month and August as additional investment is allocated to new power projects. Reflecting this, the production of electric wire and cable rose by 18% in H1 from a year earlier.  Added to this, the Shanghai Electric Wire and Cable Industry Association recently reported that the average operating rate of Shanghai wire and cable producers during H1 was above 80%. 

Elsewhere, in the construction sector house sales surged 22.5% year on year through to May.  Although this will not benefit future orders for building wire and building related copper products, as these were included in the house build stage, there is the potential for the rise in house sales to buoy future orders for copper-intensive home appliances.  Demand for home appliances has also benefitted from the government’s replacement of the home electrical appliance scheme which involves increased subsidies for consumers to replace their old home appliances in urban areas. One of the largest projects includes Chinalco Luoyang Copper’s new 100kt/a high-precision electronic copper strip and plate plant. The company recently reported that production, which is expected to begin in September this year, will reach 30kt this year before rising to full capacity in 2010. Elsewhere, Zhejiang Hailiang reported that it hopes to raise its copper alloy pipe production capacity to 260kt/a this year, up from 160kt/a currently. The increased capacity reflects the forthcoming completion of new production lines in both China and Vietnam. Capacity at its three copper alloy plants in Zhejiang will increase by 30kt/a by the end of this year while production at its Vietnam plant will increase by 70kt/a by year end. Finally, the Jinchuan Group reported this month that it expects to complete a new 60kt/a copper-nickel alloy pipe, rod and extrusion plant by the end of this year. The new 60krt/a capacity will be split as follows: 32.5kt for copper alloy rods and wire rods, 15.8kt white copper pipes, 10.7kt brass and purple pipes and 1kt extrusion products. The output will be used in shipbuilding, desalination, galvanizing, electrical appliances, automobile and military applications. The new capacity being brought on line will not only help to boost Chinese demand for copper in this year but in 2010 as well. With this is mind we continue to forecast that Chinese demand for copper will grow by 7% next year to ~6.4

Companies in the automotive and electrical and electronic sectors especially commented that demand for their products was beginning to improve. In the automotive sector both Toyota and Honda reported that they intend to bring back some weekend shifts in response to brisk orders for hybrid cars. Meanwhile, in the electrical and electronic sectors, demand is being supported by the government’s stimulus package as well as a pick up in exports to China. Shipments of wire and cable to the automotive and electrical and electronic sectors also improved during June where deliveries increased by 33% and 20.7% from May, according to the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association. However, the sharp rise was slightly misleading because many manufacturers closed their plants during May due to public holidays. On an annual basis shipments were still down; automotive wire and cable declined by 32% while wire and cable consumed within the electrical and electronic markets fell by 34.1%. Nevertheless, these declines did represent the smallest fall on an annual basis so far this year. Wire and cable shipments, overall, increased by 19.7% month on month in June but declined by 24.9% from a year earlier, according to the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association. Production of copper strip also benefitted from the improved market conditions in the automotive and electrical and electronic sectors. According to Japan’s Copper and Brass Association, output of copper strip increased by 36.8% in June from a month earlier. However, on an annual basis output was down 26.5%. Likewise with wire and cable, this represented the smallest annual decline so far in 2009. Overall the production of copper and copper alloy products increased by 22.3% from May but declined by 29.6% from June last year. China Nonferrous Metals Corp. expects to resume production at its recentlyacquired Baluba copper mine in August this year after spending $60M on refurbishing plant and equipment.  Some 600 employees have been rehired to restart the operation.  Production is expected to average 24kt/a of copper-inconcentrates and further underground development work will be required to extend the mine life and to expand output.  Meanwhile, work continues on the development of the $350M Muliashi project with commissioning of the 60kt/a SXEw operation having been earmarked for 2010. 

A recent submission of an EIS by First Quantum Minerals (FQM) has been approved by the Environmental Council of Zambia for the development of the Fishtie copper deposit, located 275km north east of Lusaka.  FQM intends to develop an open pit mine to exploit oxide ores grading 2.5% Cu at a rate of 100kt/m over a 27 month period and deliver t

hese ores to the Bwana Mkubwa SxEw facility which has been closed since running out of ore in October 2008. Mitsubishi Materials and Copper Mountain Mining have signed definitive agreements whereby Mitsubishi Materials will purchase a 25% stake in the Copper Mountain project for $28.75M, use reasonable efforts to arrange a $250M project loan and purchase all of the project’s copper concentrate output. The Copper Mountain deposit was previously mined between 1972 and 1996 and was then known as Similkameen or Similco. Long lead items have been ordered with the SAG and ball mill manufacturing underway to maintain the target production schedule for mid 2011. Detailed engineering is taking place at site and geotechnical excavation for the concentrator is now complete. Average production over the mine’s 17 year life is expected to be 40kt/a of copper-in-concentrates plus 825kg/a Au and 8.2t/a Ag. Konkola Copper Mines resumed production at its 300kt/a Nchanga smelter on July 12th after a 17 day unscheduled shutdown to effect repairs on a water cooling system in the brick wall lining of the smelter. The company hopes to bring the plant up to full capacity by October after scheduled maintenance in September. Feed for the smelter comes from KCM’s Nchanga and Konkola mines and from the nearby Lumwana and Kansanshi mines. The Government of Zambia has signed a $3.6Bn exploration agreement with Chinese mining group, Zhonghui Guohua Industries. Zhonghui will have the right to explore for copper and other minerals in the Mwinilunga area of the Northwestern Province and the Copperbelt. The company also intends to construct a 300kt/a copper smelter/refinery in the region as well as an HEP plant. Several Chinese secondary smelter/refinery projects have been in the news in recent weeks. Guangxi Nonferrous Metals Group aims to start construction of a 150kt/a scrap smelter/refinery in Wuzhou City, Guangxi province in August 2009 with first production by late 2010. Elsewhere, Jiangxi Jinhui Copper Co. has invested $65M in constructing a 100kt/a scrap smelter/refinery in Jiangxi Province and this was commissioned at the start of July.
